children: OTTAWA--Canada's goods-trade surplus with the world narrowed sharply in July with the sharpest retreat in U.S.-bound exports in more than a year and a drop in shipments of crude oil and gold.

Canada recorded a merchandise-trade surplus of 769 million Canadian dollars, the equivalent of about US$555.5 million, Statistics Canada said Thursday. That marked a fifth consecutive monthly surplus but the narrowest of the run, following an upwardly revised C$4.2 billion surplus in June.
Economists were expecting an only slightly narrowed surplus of C$3.25 billion.

After hitting the highest level on record the month before, exports of Canadian goods declined 2.3% to C$76.14 billion, while the value of imports rose 2.2% to an all-time high C$75.37 billion, a sixth straight increase, the national data agency said.

Shipments to the U.S. sank 6.6%, the sharpest pullback since April last year, while a rise in inbound passenger cars and light trucks helped lift imports from the U.S. by 1.8%. That resulted in the lowest goods-trade surplus with Canada's largest trading partner since February at C$5.91 billion from June's C$10.28 billion.

The fall in exports to the U.S. was partially countered by a 7.4% rise in shipments to other countries, the third increase in a row to reach a record high C$25.62 billion. Imports from non-U.S. countries were up 2.8%, leading to a narrowed trade deficit of C$5.14 billion with countries other than the U.S., the lowest since January 2021.
July's fall in total exports was the first in six months, led by declines in metal and mineral products and energy products. Excluding those two segments, exports rose 0.6% for the latest month.

After a nearly 16% jump in June, exports of metals and minerals fell 8.5%, driven by a fall in precious metals that was mainly due to a drop in purchases of Canadian-held gold by foreign residents and fewer shipments to the U.S.
Energy exports were down 4.4% in July, a third consecutive decline as crude fell with lower prices and volumes. Exports of natural gas were also sharply lower after rising the two previous months.
In volume terms, overall exports were down 1.5% between June and July, and imports on the same basis were up 2.2%

Trade flows were a big driver of the rebound in Canadian activity in the second quarter, with the rise in exports in recent months alongside resilient household spending helping fuel annualized growth of 3.3%, the strongest in about three years. Still, pressures have again built up that threaten to mute economic growth as fuel prices remain elevated and after the U.S. last month targeted a range of Canadian goods with new 50% tariffs.

The Bank of Canada this week left its policy interest rate unchanged for the seventh time in a row as policymakers balanced risks to inflation against headwinds to growth. Tiff Macklem, governor of the central bank, said the economy is on stronger footing after a weak start to the year and businesses are adapting to tariffs. The new tariffs aren't expected to have a large direct affect on economic activity, though uncertainty has increased and the situation remains fluid, he said.

When international trade in goods and international trade in services were combined, Canadian exports fell 1.6% in July, while imports rose 1.5%. As a result, Canada's trade surplus incorporating both goods and services narrowed to C$1.08 billion from C$4.02 billion in June.
